bites.title: Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral, and Qwen: what each is good at
bites.body:
Several families lead the open-weight field, each released by a different organisation.

Llama, from Meta, is the best known, with the widest ecosystem of tools and guides. Mistral, a French company, offers efficient models and a European base, which matters to some customers. DeepSeek, from China, drew attention for strong reasoning and coding at low cost. Qwen, from Alibaba, comes in many sizes and is strong across languages. Google's Gemma and Microsoft's Phi are small models worth knowing.

The standings move even faster here than among closed models. So learn the families as a shortlist, and check a current comparison site before choosing.

bites.title: Open weights vs. open source: always read the licence
bites.body:
"Open" is used loosely, and the differences matter.

Open weights means the trained model files are published and you can download and run them. That is all it means.

Open source, in the proper sense, means you may use, change and share the thing for any purpose. Many open-weight models do not go that far. The training data and training code are usually not released, and the licence may carry conditions.

Think of a restaurant that hands you the finished dish to take home, compared with one that gives you the recipe and lets you sell it.

The only way to know what you have is the licence text. "It is on the internet" is not permission.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

choices.text: That you may use it for any purpose without conditions

questions.explanation: Open weights means the files are published. What you may do with them depends on the licence.

bites.title: Licences can limit large companies or certain uses; check each one
bites.body:
Model licences vary a great deal, and the conditions can bite.

Some are fully permissive, such as Apache 2.0 and MIT: use them commercially, change them, no strings beyond giving credit.

Others are custom "community" licences with conditions. Typical ones: limits above a certain number of users or amount of revenue, bans on particular uses, rules about naming, or "research only, no commercial use".

The same family can use different licences for different versions and sizes, so last year's check does not cover this year's release.

Read it like a rental agreement before moving in. For client or commercial work, record which model, which version and which licence you relied on.

bites.title: Sizes: small models run on a laptop; the largest need data-centre hardware
bites.body:
Open models come in sizes, counted in parameters, and size decides where they can run.

Small, up to about 8 billion parameters: runs on a good laptop or even a phone. Quick, private and limited.

Medium, tens of billions: needs a strong desktop with a serious graphics card, or a rented cloud machine.

Large, hundreds of billions: needs several data-centre GPUs, each costing as much as a car.

The thing to check is memory. The model has to fit in the graphics card's memory. A trick called quantisation shrinks a model by storing its numbers less precisely, like saving a photo as a smaller JPEG. You lose a little quality and it fits on cheaper hardware.

Adds more parameters

questions.explanation: Lower-precision numbers make the model smaller and cheaper to run, with a modest quality loss.

bites.title: Strengths: control, privacy, lower cost at volume, and fine-tuning
bites.body:
Open-weight models earn their place in four situations.

Control: the model does not change unless you change it. No surprise retirement and no silent update.

Privacy: run it on your own machines and no data leaves the building. For some clients and regulators that settles the matter.

Cost at volume: for steady, heavy workloads, running your own can beat paying per token. At low volume it is usually dearer.

Fine-tuning: you can retrain the model freely on your own data.

It is owning a van instead of using couriers. If you ship all day every day, it makes sense. For one parcel a week, it does not.

bites.title: Weaknesses: you own the setup, updates, and safety
bites.body:
With an open model, everything the provider used to do becomes your job.

Setup: choosing hardware, installing the serving software, getting acceptable speed. Operations: keeping it running, handling busy periods, fixing it at night. Updates: nobody improves your copy, so better versions are yours to find, test and install. Safety: the filters and abuse monitoring a provider bundles in are yours to add.

And for the hardest tasks, the best open model usually trails the best closed one.

It is owning a house instead of renting. Nobody raises the rent, and when the boiler fails, you are the one who gets the call.

The token price may be zero. The engineer's time is not.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high
